Framework Documentation
The Adaptive Convexity Framework

Part 1 of 6 · ≈ 18 min read · In pictures · 8 exhibits →

Foundation & Philosophy

Manifesto

The traditional portfolio playbook is failing quietly.

It was built for a world where inflation came in episodes, correlations held still, bonds could be counted on to cushion stocks, and volatility was an inconvenience to be averaged away. In that world diversification did most of the work. An advisor could rebalance on a calendar and collect a fee, and the approach held up because the regime was cooperating. Risk meant standard deviation, prices were expected to drift back to their averages, and the 60/40 portfolio passed for the sensible default.

The 2020s look different. Regimes shift, markets and policymakers react to each other, and means calm and storm arrive in runs rather than evenly spaced. Central banks are torn between fighting inflation and keeping the financial system stable, and cannot always do both. Geopolitics is fragmenting as the post–Cold War order splits into competing blocs. Technology keeps pushing the prices of many goods down even as asset prices climb, so the consumer price index and the cost of owning things drift apart. And public debt has become, in the framework’s reading, a constraint on policy instead of a footnote. Economists call that condition : the point at which the cost of carrying the debt starts to limit what a central bank can do.

Volatility is the risk everyone sees. The quieter one is falling behind while the statement says you are fine. Consumer prices rose about 88 percent from the end of 1999 to the end of 2024. Home prices more than tripled. An equal mix of stocks (with dividends), homes, and gold rose about sixfold.

Some of that gap is real growth and falling interest rates, so not all of it is inflation. It still shows how far a portfolio judged only against CPI could fall behind the assets it could have owned. Falling rates did something less visible too: they let the US government borrow more without paying more. From 1991 to 2021, federal debt held by the public more than doubled as a share of GDP (about 44 to 94 percent) while falling rates cut the interest bill by more than half (3.2 to 1.5 percent of GDP). By 2025 the bill was back at about 3.2 percent of GDP, level with its 1991 peak, on more than twice the debt.

A portfolio tuned for average conditions turns when conditions stop being average. Fragility and volatility are different things. A portfolio that drops 15 percent in a routine correction and then recovers is volatile but sound. A portfolio that takes a permanent loss when its diversifiers all fall at once, in a , is fragile. The difference lives in how the holdings behave together under stress, which an average volatility figure does not show.

The hedge most portfolios leaned on belonged to one period. For about two decades, from roughly 2000 to 2021, stocks and bonds tended to move in opposite directions, so bonds cushioned equity losses. From about 1970 to the late 1990s the correlation was usually positive, and in 2021 and 2022 it turned positive again.

In 2022 a 60/40 mix of US stocks and bonds fell about 16 percent: stocks lost about 18 percent with dividends, and bonds, the part meant to cushion them, lost about 13 percent. That broke the assumption that bonds hedge stocks. For a retiree drawing 4 percent a year, a loss like that early in retirement is worse than a bad year, because withdrawals taken from a shrunken balance leave less to recover with. That is , and in 2022 it left the textbooks and turned up in real accounts. Bad luck had little to do with it, and so did “this time is different.” The portfolio was built for a regime that had ended.

A hedge earns the name by holding up under stress. Here is 2022, drawn through the year.

Over the same years, some holdings that conventional advice files under speculative or unsuitable built wealth for those who could hold them, Bitcoin above all, though never smoothly. Bitcoin fell more than 70 percent twice, in 2018 and again in 2021 and 2022. The second fall, from its November 2021 high to its November 2022 low, was about 77 percent. Buying a fixed amount every month from January 2018 to December 2024, through both falls, still ended at about seven times the money put in. That only works for a position small enough that nothing forces a sale at the bottom. Among ordinary equities, the winners were the ones that matched the regime: energy was the S&P 500’s best sector in 2022, returning about 66 percent with dividends while the index lost about 18 percent, and information technology, with AI-related names leading, returned about 58 percent in 2023.

In hindsight, the period rewarded investors whose positions matched the regime and were sized to survive the falls along the way. That illustrates the argument; it does not prove that regime calls can be made reliably in advance, which is why the framework spends as much effort on surviving a wrong call as on making a right one.

So the Adaptive Convexity Framework starts from a different premise:

The objective of portfolio management is not prediction. It is survivable compounding under uncertainty.

A prediction names an outcome: Bitcoin at $150,000 by a set date, or the Federal Reserve cutting rates in a set sequence. Predictions are brittle. They come out right or wrong, the wrong ones tend to be expensive, and even a forecast that gets the direction right can miss on timing. Timing decides whether a position lives long enough for its thesis to be proved.

Timing matters most once you are drawing on the portfolio, because withdrawals make the order of returns count. Same returns, same withdrawals, different order. At a 4 percent withdrawal, losses first ends with less than half what gains first ends with; at 6 percent it runs out in year 12.

means building a portfolio that can be wrong about timing, size or specific outcomes and still be standing, while keeping enough exposure to payoffs, the kind where being right pays far more than being wrong costs. With payoffs shaped that way, being right only some of the time can still compound to far more than a risk-free return would.

Here is that shape, and it is not free: near the middle, the curved line sits a little below a plain straight-line bet. That is the price of the bend. Sizing keeps the left side survivable, and the right side is left open, within the concentration limits.

The framework treats investing as a system rather than a set of static allocations. It draws on practical macro investing, the mathematics of convexity and portfolio construction theory. The method carries across account types and investor profiles; the tax material is written for US accounts under current law. It is built to be audited: each decision should trace to a written rule or a recorded judgment, so you can explain it to an advisor, a client or an heir. That is a design goal, not a legal standard.

It has seven components, each aimed at a known way traditional portfolios fail:

  1. A macro thesis

    formed and tested by the practitioner, that frames the regime and informs structure, against the failure mode of allocating as if the regime did not matter

  2. A Bitcoin backbone

    sized and paced by valuation discipline, with the as one of its lenses, against two failure modes: holding none, which gives up the convexity, and holding too much without rules, which invites ruin

  3. Tax wrappers

    treated as compounding engines rather than paperwork, against the failure mode of careless account placement, which can cost a large share of terminal wealth

  4. Portfolio construction

    expressed through each position’s and its (, , ), against the failure mode of thinking in asset classes without asking how a holding behaves in the regime

  5. Convexity

    governed by scoring, against the failure mode of holding a deteriorating position out of attachment or sunk cost

  6. Momentum

    as a trend filter and a governor on drawdowns, against the failure mode of fighting the prevailing trend or riding a position through a catastrophic fall

  7. Predefined tripwires and AI-assisted verification

    as the control system, against the failure modes of scarce attention and information overload

Bitcoin is in the portfolio for what it does, not as an article of faith. It is a long-duration monetary asset that runs parallel to the dollar system, with valuation lenses you can measure, growing institutional access, a supply capped by its protocol, and several cycles of lopsided compounding through severe volatility. It is scored like every other holding, but sized and handled under its own rules (Part 3). Part 3 also makes the full case for owning it and sets out the valuation models that pace it: network growth, adoption curves and sensitivity to liquidity.

Account placement stops being a compliance chore and becomes a return lever, especially for strategies whose returns come from a few large wins. Over decades, where a convex holding sits (Roth, taxable, or pre-tax) can change what you keep by a wide margin; Parts 4 and 5 work the arithmetic and state their assumptions. At equal tax rates in and out, Roth and pre-tax end even. For convex, positions the balance tips toward Roth because contribution limits are set in dollars, required distributions can push large pre-tax balances into higher brackets, and heirs generally inherit a Roth free of income tax under current law (Part 4).

What follows is a written doctrine meant to replace static allocation with a process you can adapt and audit. It forecasts no specific outcome and guarantees no return. It aims to compound through regimes nobody can reliably predict while keeping whatever convexity is on offer. Some policy paths or regime changes may still invalidate parts of its positioning; the framework is built to notice when that happens and respond. If you are building wealth for your own family, it gives you a repeatable process. If you advise others, it offers a documented alternative to fee-for-beta management, though not a substitute for your own suitability process.

Abstract

A portfolio operating system for unstable regimes.

The Adaptive Convexity Framework is a portfolio operating system for unstable macro regimes, the kind marked by policy reflexivity, volatility clustering, lopsided outcomes and correlations that will not hold still. It anchors long-horizon conviction in Bitcoin, valued with power-law corridors and several independent models drawn from network growth, adoption curves, liquidity sensitivity and on-chain data. Positions are rated by the Convexity Integrity Score (), a weighted scoring heuristic that scores each position at each weekly review, and between reviews when a trigger fires, across four components: convexity and optionality, risk and fragility, macro alignment, and execution and sentiment. The score is there to catch narrative drift, sunk-cost thinking and positions kept on rationalization. Part 6 sets out the method.

are treated as a return lever, and placement follows what each holding is expected to do. Torque that may rotate is directed to Roth. Taxable accounts hold never-sold Bitcoin, return-of-capital Ballast and positions kept for tax-loss harvesting. Pre-tax contributions are tactical: used in an unusually high-income year, or to capture an employer match. Step 2 below gives the routing, and Part 4 works it through.

Risk is managed through predefined , written when the thesis is set, around the regime’s dominant fragilities: systemic stress indicators such as bond-market volatility (MOVE), liquidity conditions, breadth and credit spreads, and position-level signals such as CIS decay, momentum breakdown and valuation extension. The dashboard watches the ones it has data for and displays each tripwire’s prescribed response; it never executes one (as of September 2026). Tripwires are paired with a verification step the practitioner runs, with AI-assisted research, to speed adaptation without inducing overtrading.

Borrowing against appreciated assets, through securities-backed lines of credit or Bitcoin-backed loans, can supply cash instead of a sale, and under current US law assets held until death generally pass to heirs with a stepped-up basis. That is the pattern, taught in Part 3. The loan avoids the sale, but it adds interest cost and the risk of a forced sale: if the collateral falls far enough, or a payment is missed, the lender sells it, and that sale is a taxable event. Every position outside the Bitcoin backbone carries a posture (Torque, Ballast or Hype), which lets the portfolio rotate across themes such as AI infrastructure, defense modernization, space commercialization, critical systems and biotechnology as the evolves.

The result is a documented doctrine built to express a range of macro theses while keeping convexity, staying survivable through drawdowns and compounding tax-efficiently over decades. Static allocations are tuned for average conditions and degrade when regimes change; this framework is built to adapt. It is designed to be wrong gracefully, to catch thesis breaks early and to redeploy capital by rule rather than by mood. The framework draws on Taleb’s fragility mathematics, Druckenmiller’s concentration discipline paired with active monitoring, Soros’s reflexivity dynamics, and Edelman’s longevity horizon work.

Order of Operations

The system at a glance.

  1. Macro thesis
  2. Bitcoin backbone
  3. Tax architecture
  4. Portfolio construction
  5. CIS governance
  6. Momentum filter
  7. Tripwires
  8. Verification
  9. Adapt & compound

The method runs in a fixed order, and the order matters because each stage depends on the one before it. Build a portfolio without a macro thesis and you get exposure with no structure. Size Bitcoin without valuation discipline and you either miss the opportunity or take on ruin risk, depending on which way you erred. Allocate without a wrapper plan and you can give away a large share of terminal wealth. Skip CIS scoring and narrative drift creeps in. Ignore momentum and drawdowns tend to run deeper and take longer to recover. Run without tripwires and thesis breaks get noticed late. Skip verification and decisions made in volatile weeks lean on emotion.

CIS and momentum work as a pair. CIS rates the position; momentum checks whether the market agrees. Neither outranks the other, and together they decide how much capital a position may carry.

The nine steps, in order:

  1. Macro thesis determines structure. If the operative thesis is the Fourth Turning (the crisis era in William Strauss and Neil Howe’s generational-cycle theory, which the framework reads through debt dynamics and generational change), structure tilts toward defense, critical infrastructure, parallel systems and hard assets. If it is a disinflationary technology boom (AI raising productivity, goods prices falling, asset prices rising), structure tilts toward AI infrastructure, semiconductors, cloud computing and technology platforms. Real theses often blend the two; the example thesis in Part 2 combines the Fourth Turning reading of history with AI infrastructure buildout, fiscal dominance and liquidity-driven asset cycles. A thesis makes no point forecast. It is a lens for reading signals and spreading probability across regime scenarios. Whatever the thesis, Bitcoin is held as the backbone, sized and paced under the rules in Part 3.

  2. Structure determines wrapper placement. Torque that may rotate is directed to Roth accounts, where right-tail outcomes (which can reach 10 to 100 times the initial position) compound and rotate tax-free. Taxable accounts hold never-sold Bitcoin, return-of-capital Ballast, buy-and-hold positions beyond Roth capacity, and smaller satellite positions kept for tax-loss harvesting. Pre-tax accounts take the employer match, a deferral in an unusually high-income year, and ordinary-income payers such as bond funds where pre-tax space exists. On the match: contribute at least enough to earn the full employer match. Your own contribution can go into a Roth 401(k) bucket if the plan has one. The match itself is pre-tax unless the plan lets you elect Roth matching contributions, which SECURE 2.0 permits if the plan adopts it (the match must be fully vested and is taxable income in the year it is made). Placement follows what each holding is expected to do, held for good or rotated, and Part 4 sets out the full map.

  3. Wrapper placement decides what a size is worth. Sizing bands are set by posture and conviction, through the CIS-to-allocation tables in Part 5, and concentration limits apply to the household total across every account. Placement then decides how much of a given size you keep: the same position compounds without tax drag in a Roth, while in a taxable account tax and the cost of realizing gains shrink the retained outcome.

  4. CIS selects the sizing band. Every position is scored on convexity and optionality, risk and fragility, macro alignment, and execution and sentiment. For every holding except the Bitcoin backbone, posture sets the band table. The score selects the posture-specific sizing band: 70 or above supports core sizing, 60 to 69 standard sizing, 50 to 59 starter sizing, and below 50 is not allocation-worthy. A material score change prompts a resizing review; at 50 and above, exits are governed by posture rules, tripwires and thesis evidence, not by the score band alone. Part 6 develops the full rubric and its weights. The step exists to stop “I like this stock” portfolio construction.

  5. CIS scores are confirmed by momentum. The reads the market’s vote on the thesis on three dimensions: distance from the 52-week high, strength relative to the sector and the market, and breadth. A position with CIS 75 and one broken momentum dimension has its sizing reduced 25 to 30 percent; with two broken it goes on watch with minimal new exposure; with all three broken (extended distance below the 52-week high, negative relative strength, declining breadth) it exits despite the score, per Part 5. CIS below 50 removes allocation eligibility at any momentum reading. The dashboard does not yet measure the three dimensions (as of September 2026); Part 5 says what it watches instead.

  6. Momentum is monitored by tripwires. Tripwires are engineered during thesis optimization around the regime’s dominant fragilities. For the current thesis, the systemic set watches bond-market volatility (the MOVE index), equity volatility (the VIX), market breadth and widening credit spreads; at the position level, a sharp CIS decline, a drawdown limit and a momentum breakdown. Different theses produce different tripwire sets; a deflationary thesis, for example, might monitor M2 contraction and yield-curve dynamics instead. The thresholds the dashboard watches are on the Math page, and Part 5 sets the responses. Tripwires convert passive monitoring into active governance.

  7. Tripwires trigger verification. When a tripwire fires, the next step is verification: is the signal noise (temporary volatility) or information (a thesis break)? That step is the practitioner’s, with where it helps: news flow, positioning data, sentiment indicators and historical analogs. The dashboard helps in one way today: its AI market briefing (Tape Read) reads the current tripwire states when you run it. Nothing launches research automatically when a tripwire fires. Human judgment makes the call.

  8. Verification informs adaptation. What verification finds sorts the response into one of four categories: watch (thesis intact, volatility normal), hedge (thesis weakening), trim (thesis breaking, reduce by 25 to 50 percent), or exit and redeploy (thesis broken, move the capital to higher-CIS opportunities). Deciding the categories in advance is what keeps a bad week from writing its own response.

  9. Adaptation feeds back into the macro thesis. When several positions in a theme breach CIS thresholds at the same time despite strong momentum, the thesis itself may be shifting. The framework updates its operating assumptions as that evidence accumulates.

Key Insight

This is a closed loop. Rules drive most decisions, recorded judgment drives the rest, and both leave a trail: every action should trace to a trigger and be logged. The framework is built to reduce error, and to fail gracefully when a regime breaks its assumptions.

Drawn as a single picture, the loop is small enough to hold in your head: a thesis earns exposure, exposure creates risk, a tripwire stands guard, and the governed response feeds what it learns back into the thesis. The nine steps above are this loop with the detail filled in.

Six failure modes turn up again and again, and each has a named answer in the framework:

Narrative drift

Holding a deteriorating position because “I still believe in the story.” CIS forces a scored reassessment.

Recency bias

Overweighting recent winners or panic-selling recent losers. Momentum filters and tripwires set the rules before the panic arrives.

Fragility to correlation shifts

Assuming diversification holds under stress. A barbell structure and return-of-capital Ballast are meant to keep working when correlations jump.

Tax inefficiency

Putting holdings in whichever account had room, and losing terminal wealth to tax. Account placement is a design decision from the first dollar.

Attention scarcity

Missing thesis breaks under information overload. Tripwires watch the critical signals for you.

Emotional decision-making

Buying tops, selling bottoms, chasing performance. Written rules stand in for the impulse of the moment.

Treating each decision as the output of a governed process takes discretion away where it does damage (emotional sizing, holding on a narrative, ignoring tax) and leaves it where it adds value (thematic rotation, tactical positioning and adaptive use of borrowing).

None of this removes judgment. It gives judgment less noise to fight through. You still make every decision, inside a structure built to prevent catastrophic errors without locking out adaptation.

Survival comes first because only capital that survives can keep compounding. The closing picture draws a path like the Bitcoin one described earlier: a fixed amount bought every month, straight through two deep falls.

Scope

The framework is a designed process, not a fitted model. Its rules and scores have not been backtested against a benchmark; where these pages describe outcomes, they describe what the design intends unless a figure is labeled as measured. Apart from Part 1’s sequence-of-returns exhibit, the worked examples in these Parts assume you are not yet drawing on the portfolio. The framework does not yet publish a withdrawal policy for a portfolio you live on. Tax and borrowing treatments are described under current US law as of September 2026 and can change. This framework does not constitute investment, tax, or legal advice.
